skill: Explaining the functional role of the Data Date in a P6 schedule update
question: In Primavera P6, what does the Data Date represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The date the project file was originally created in P6

options.label: B
options.text: The as-of status date that separates recorded actual progress from forecast/remaining work

options.label: C
options.text: The contractual completion date stated in the baseline

options.label: D
options.text: The date the last cost budget was approved by the client

explanation: The Data Date (DD) is the status/as-of date for the whole schedule: everything at or before it is treated as historical fact (actual dates, actual duration, progress recorded), and everything from it forward is forecast, produced by the forward and backward pass. It has nothing to do with when the file was created and is not itself a contractual date.
reasoning: P6's scheduling algorithm anchors the forward pass for incomplete activities at the Data Date (or later, if constrained) and treats actual dates on or before it as fixed history. Every update cycle, DD is advanced to the new as-of date before the schedule is recalculated.
commonMistakes: Treating Data Date as a fixed project start date.
Confusing Data Date with the contractual completion date.
Assuming Data Date only affects reports, not the actual date/float calculation.
redFlags: Cannot explain that DD divides actual from forecast in the calculation itself, not just visually.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to the forecast start dates of not-yet-started activities if the Data Date is never advanced during a live project?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate connects DD mechanics to real update discipline rather than reciting a definition.

skill: Sequencing the correct steps of a periodic P6 status update and explaining why order matters
scenario: It is the last working day of the reporting month on a mid-rise commercial office project. You have field progress input from every subcontractor foreman, and by Monday morning you must issue the updated P6 schedule.
question: Describe, in the correct order, the steps you would carry out to produce a technically sound monthly update, and explain why that order matters.
expectedAnswer: Move the Data Date forward to the period-end status date; enter Actual Start/Actual Finish and progress (remaining duration and/or % complete per the project's percent-complete-type policy) for every activity based on validated field input; incorporate any separately-approved logic or scope changes; run Schedule (F9); then review the results for out-of-sequence progress, negative float, and constraint conflicts before comparing to baseline and issuing.
strongAnswer: Explains that DD must be set to the new status date before or as part of statusing, because P6 treats everything at/before DD as actual and everything after as forecast — entering actuals inconsistent with a stale DD produces anomalies (dates that appear to be in the future relative to DD, wrong out-of-sequence flags). Also separates pure status entry from logic/scope changes so the two effects aren't conflated when explaining variance later.
expertAnswer: Adds that a schedule health check (logic density, hard constraints, high-float/dangling activities, negative float) should be run every cycle, not just before major submittals, and that the updated schedule should be reconciled against the progress S-curve/earned value before it is issued, since a schedule can calculate cleanly and still misrepresent physical progress.
explanation: There is a defensible standard order: set the new Data Date, status activities against field-verified facts, apply approved changes separately, recalculate, then diagnose. Doing these out of order corrupts the result — for example, running the schedule calculation before entering progress recalculates remaining work against last period's status, and entering actual dates before moving the Data Date can create actuals that appear to post-date the status point.
reasoning: P6's forward pass for remaining work starts at the Data Date. If DD has not yet been advanced when new actual dates are entered, those actuals can sit later than DD, which P6 flags as an inconsistency and which corrupts the out-of-sequence detection used later in the process. Sequencing status before logic changes also keeps the story clean when a client or PM later asks 'why did the finish date move this month.'
commonMistakes: Running Schedule (F9) before entering the period's actual progress, so remaining work recalculates against stale status.
Forgetting to move the Data Date at all, so newly entered actuals appear inconsistent with the status point.
Mixing logic or resequencing changes into the same pass as pure status entry without flagging them, making variance impossible to explain later.
redFlags: No structured process at all — 'I just enter whatever field call comes in, in whatever order it arrives.'
Cannot explain why moving the Data Date matters.
p6Checks: Schedule (F9) dialog — confirm the new Data Date is set before recalculating.
Activities view, filter for 'Activities with out-of-sequence progress' after recalculation.
Schedule Log / Scheduling Report for negative float and open ends after the run.

followUpQuestions.prompt: A junior planner argues it's faster to enter all progress first and move the Data Date last, right before running the schedule. Is that acceptable?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands DD-before-entry vs DD-just-before-calculation are both workable as long as DD precedes the F9 run, not whether they've memorized one rigid ritual.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would you do differently on a schedule with resource-leveling turned on?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness that leveling recalculates dates based on resource availability and should be sequenced deliberately, not run accidentally mid-update.

dimensions.guidance: Names the correct, complete sequence of real steps.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Explains why the order matters mechanically, not just recites it.

dimensions.name: completeness
dimensions.guidance: Covers status entry, approved changes, recalculation, and post-run review as distinct steps.

skill: Distinguishing the Data Date from the completion status of individual activities
question: True or False: The Data Date must always be set equal to the Actual Finish date of the most recently completed activity in the schedule.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: The Data Date is a single project-wide status date chosen by the update cycle (e.g., the last day of the reporting period), not derived from any one activity's Actual Finish. Activities can finish on many different dates within a period; the Data Date is simply the as-of point at which the whole schedule is being statused, and it can fall after the most recent Actual Finish, on the same date, or (for a same-day close-out) coincide with it.
reasoning: Conflating DD with an individual activity's Actual Finish is a common junior error that leads to setting the Data Date too early (e.g., to the date of the last-recorded finish rather than the true period end), which then understates elapsed time and misrepresents how much of the update period has actually passed for schedule health and forecasting.
commonMistakes: Setting Data Date to the latest Actual Finish in the schedule rather than the agreed reporting cut-off.

Believing every activity must finish on or before the exact Data Date value with no exceptions (in practice, this is enforced as a rule, but the DD itself is chosen independently, not derived from activity data).
redFlags: Cannot separate 'when did work finish' from 'what date are we reporting as of'.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If Data Date isn't derived from any single activity, who or what determines it each period?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Redirects toward the real answer: the reporting cycle/contract requirement sets it.

skill: Recognizing valid vs invalid combinations of Actual Start, Actual Finish, and % Complete
scenario: An activity in a warehouse fit-out schedule has an Actual Start date entered, no Actual Finish date, and shows 0% Complete after the update.
question: Is this a valid, self-consistent state for the activity, or does it indicate a data problem? Explain.
expectedAnswer: It is technically valid — once an Actual Start is entered the activity's status becomes In Progress/Started, and % Complete legitimately can be 0% in the very early part of execution (e.g., the crew mobilized on site but has not yet produced measurable output). It is not automatically an error.
strongAnswer: Notes that while valid, it should prompt a sanity check: how long ago was the Actual Start relative to the current Data Date? If the gap is large (e.g., started three weeks ago, still 0%), that is a red flag worth investigating even though the data combination itself is legal.
explanation: P6 does not require % Complete to be greater than zero the moment Actual Start is entered — status simply moves from Not Started to In Progress. The combination becomes suspicious, not invalid, when the elapsed time since Actual Start is large relative to the activity's duration with no progress recorded.
reasoning: Status logic in P6: Not Started = no Actual Start; In Progress = Actual Start set, Actual Finish blank; Completed = both set. % Complete is an independent data point layered on top of that state, so 'Started, 0%' is a legitimate early-execution snapshot, not a contradiction.
commonMistakes: Assuming any non-zero Actual Duration must force % Complete above zero.
Flagging the record as a definite data-entry error rather than a state that is valid but worth a follow-up question.
redFlags: States with certainty that this combination is impossible in P6.
p6Checks: Activities view, compare Actual Start to Data Date to gauge elapsed time.
Check Remaining Duration — if it still equals the full Original Duration, confirm that's a deliberate 'mobilized, not yet producing' status rather than an overlooked update.

followUpQuestions.prompt: At what point would you start treating 'Started, still 0%' as a genuine problem rather than normal early-stage status?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests judgment about proportionality, not just the binary valid/invalid answer.

dimensions.name: technicalAccuracy
dimensions.guidance: Correctly identifies the combination as valid, not an error.

dimensions.name: professionalJudgment
dimensions.guidance: Recognizes when the same valid combination should still trigger a follow-up question.

skill: Determining the correct P6 status entries for multiple activities from raw field progress input, including recognizing an out-of-sequence condition
scenario:
Riverside Heights is a 32-storey residential tower. The prior monthly update had a Data Date of 2026-06-30. It is now 2026-07-31, and you have collected the following field-verified information for four Level 18 activities:
- 'Column Formwork & Rebar - Zone A' (Original Duration 6d): was Not Started at the June update; the field report confirms the crew started 2026-07-06 and the pour inspection was signed off complete on 2026-07-13.
- 'Slab Formwork - Zone A' (Original Duration 10d): was In Progress, 40% physical complete, 6 days Remaining Duration as of 2026-06-30. As of 2026-07-31 the foreman reports about 90% of the rebar and formwork is placed, with an estimated 1 more working day needed to finish, but no sign-off yet.
- 'Concrete Pour - Slab Zone A' (Original Duration 1d; FS predecessor: Slab Formwork - Zone A): was Not Started at the June update. To keep the tower-crane climb schedule intact, the site poured a 20% strip of the slab on 2026-07-28 even though formwork on the remaining 80% of the zone was not yet complete.
- 'MEP Sleeves & Embeds - Zone A' (Original Duration 4d): was Not Started at the June update and remains untouched; the subcontractor has not mobilized.
requiredAnalysis: For each activity, determine the correct Actual Start, Actual Finish, Remaining Duration and/or % Complete entries, and identify which activity needs special handling once the schedule is recalculated.
question: For each of the four activities, state exactly what you would enter in P6 at the 2026-07-31 update (Actual Start, Actual Finish, Remaining Duration and/or % Complete as applicable). Then identify which activity will require special handling once you run the schedule calculation, and explain why.
expectedDecision: Column Formwork & Rebar - Zone A: Actual Start 2026-07-06, Actual Finish 2026-07-13, 100% complete, Remaining Duration 0. Slab Formwork - Zone A: no Actual Finish yet; Remaining Duration re-forecast to 1 day based on the foreman's bottom-up estimate (not mechanically derived from elapsed time), % Complete updated to reflect genuine physical progress rather than assumed from duration elapsed. Concrete Pour - Slab Zone A: Actual Start 2026-07-28, a % Complete reflecting the roughly 20% poured, Remaining Duration re-forecast for the remaining ~80% of the pour — and this activity is the one needing special handling: it now shows progress against an unfinished predecessor (Slab Formwork - Zone A is not yet 100%), which is an out-of-sequence progress condition that P6 will flag on recalculation. MEP Sleeves & Embeds - Zone A: no change, remains Not Started with its original 4-day duration intact (assuming no replan).
expectedAnswer: Correctly states the four sets of entries and identifies the Concrete Pour activity as out-of-sequence because it has recorded actual progress ahead of a predecessor relationship that has not yet been satisfied.
strongAnswer: Explains that the Data Date must be moved to 2026-07-31 as part of this update, that Remaining Duration should come from the foreman's bottom-up estimate rather than a mechanical original-minus-elapsed calculation, and correctly names the P6 term 'out-of-sequence progress' for the pour activity.
expertAnswer: Adds that the out-of-sequence condition should not simply be left to whichever Retained Logic/Progress Override setting the project happens to use — the planner should confirm with site that the remaining 80% of the pour genuinely still needs the outstanding formwork finished before it proceeds (i.e., the real-world logic constraint still applies to the unexecuted portion), and should consider documenting the reason for the sequence break (crane-climb recovery decision) so it doesn't read as an uncontrolled logic violation in a later schedule audit.
explanation: This is a realistic monthly cycle: three activities are simple actual-progress entries, and one activity shows genuine execution ahead of its planned logic. The core test is recognizing the fourth case as out-of-sequence progress rather than just another normal update, and re-forecasting Slab Formwork's remaining duration from the foreman's estimate rather than assuming linear time-based progress.
reasoning: Out-of-sequence progress occurs whenever a successor has recorded actual progress while its predecessor relationship has not yet been satisfied per the network logic. Here the concrete pour (successor via a Finish-to-Start relationship) has an Actual Start before its predecessor's Actual Finish, which is the textbook trigger. Remaining Duration should always be a bottom-up forecast of what is genuinely left to do, not a formula applied blindly to elapsed calendar time.
commonMistakes: Entering the pour's progress without noticing it violates the predecessor relationship.
Setting Slab Formwork's Remaining Duration by simple proportion (e.g., '4 days used out of 10, so 6 remaining') instead of the foreman's field estimate.
Marking Column Formwork & Rebar 100% complete without entering an Actual Finish date.
redFlags: Does not recognize the out-of-sequence condition at all.
Treats all four activities as routine, mechanically identical status entries.
p6Checks: Activities view, filter 'Activities with out-of-sequence progress' after recalculating with the new Data Date.
Check the project's Schedule Options for Retained Logic vs Progress Override before interpreting the pour activity's forecast dates.
Confirm Remaining Duration on Slab Formwork was overwritten with the foreman's 1-day estimate, not left at a stale prior value.

skill: Calculating Duration % Complete from Actual Duration and Remaining Duration
scenario: An activity 'Pipe Rack Steel Erection' has an Original Duration of 18 working days. At the current update, its Actual Duration (elapsed working days since Actual Start, per the activity calendar) is 12 days, and the site engineer estimates 3 working days of erection work remain.
question: Using P6's Duration % Complete formula (Actual Duration divided by At Completion Duration), calculate the activity's Duration % Complete at this update. Show your calculation.
explanation: At Completion Duration = Actual Duration + Remaining Duration = 12 + 3 = 15 days. Duration % Complete = Actual Duration / At Completion Duration x 100 = 12 / 15 x 100 = 80%. Note that At Completion Duration (15 days) is now less than the Original Duration (18 days) because the remaining estimate came in below the original plan for the unexecuted portion — this is a normal, valid outcome once Remaining Duration is re-forecast rather than mechanically derived from Original Duration.
reasoning: P6's Duration % Complete is purely a function of Actual Duration and Remaining Duration, not the Original Duration directly. Once Remaining Duration is re-forecast by the field team, At Completion Duration and therefore Duration % Complete change accordingly, independent of what the plan originally assumed.
commonMistakes: Using Original Duration (18) as the denominator instead of At Completion Duration (15), giving an incorrect 66.7%.
Forgetting that Duration % Complete is a calculated field, not something typed directly, when the activity's Percent Complete Type is set to Duration.
redFlags: Cannot explain what At Completion Duration means.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: confirm Percent Complete Type is set to Duration before relying on this formula.
Verify Remaining Duration was re-forecast by the field team rather than left at a stale prior value.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the site engineer's 3-day remaining estimate later proves optimistic and the true remaining work takes 6 more days, what happens to Duration % Complete at the following update, and is that a problem?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that Duration % Complete is not monotonic in a simple sense and can be revised as forecasts change.

skill: Distinguishing what Actual Duration measures from what Remaining Duration measures during status entry
scenario: A new planner on a highway resurfacing project tells you: 'I updated the Actual Duration field to show how many days of work are left on the milling activity.'
question: What is wrong with this statement, and what would you check first to correct the planner's understanding?
expectedAnswer: Actual Duration represents elapsed working time already consumed (from Actual Start to Data Date, or to Actual Finish if complete) — it is historical, not a field for entering remaining work. Remaining Duration is the separate field for how much work is left. The planner has the two concepts reversed.
strongAnswer: Notes that Actual Duration is generally system-calculated from the calendar once Actual Start and Data Date (or Actual Finish) are known, not something a planner should be typing directly to represent forecast work, and explains the correct field to edit is Remaining Duration.
explanation: Actual Duration answers 'how much calendar time has this activity already consumed,' while Remaining Duration answers 'how much more time is genuinely needed to finish.' Confusing the two typically results in a corrupted At Completion Duration and a distorted % Complete.
reasoning: At Completion Duration = Actual Duration + Remaining Duration. If a planner enters forecast remaining work into the Actual Duration field, the split between historical and forecast time collapses, producing % Complete and forecast finish dates that don't reflect reality.
commonMistakes: Treating Actual Duration as an editable forecast field.
Not checking which field actually drives the forward pass for remaining work (Remaining Duration does).
redFlags: Cannot explain the difference between the two fields at all.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: confirm which field (Actual Duration vs Remaining Duration) the planner actually edited.
Check the resulting At Completion Duration and % Complete for the activity to see if they now look distorted.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate treats a data-entry error as something to quietly fix or something to transparently correct and document.

subcategory: Physical % vs Duration % vs Units % Complete
skill: Correctly characterizing the three P6 percent-complete types and when each is appropriate
question: Which of the following statements about P6's three Percent Complete Types (Physical, Duration, Units) are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: Duration % Complete is calculated automatically from Actual Duration and Remaining Duration and is inherently time-based, not output-based.

options.label: B
options.text: Physical % Complete is entered independently and does not automatically drive Remaining Duration, which is why it is generally preferred for earned value reporting when backed by an objective quantities-tracking system.

options.label: C
options.text: Units % Complete is based on actual vs at-completion resource/labor units and ties naturally into cost and productivity tracking.

options.label: D
options.text: All three percent-complete types always produce an identical percentage for a given activity, because they are just different display formats of the same underlying number.

options.label: E
options.text: Physical % Complete is inherently more objective than Duration % Complete purely because it exists as a separate field, regardless of whether it is backed by measured quantities.

explanation: The three percent-complete types measure genuinely different things and can diverge substantially on the same activity: Duration % Complete tracks elapsed time consumed, Units % Complete tracks resource/labor effort consumed, and Physical % Complete is an independent, manually entered measure meant to represent true physical output. Physical % Complete is only more reliable when it is disciplined and tied to an objective measurement basis (quantities installed, milestones achieved, weighted steps) — simply existing as a separate field does not make it objective; an unsupported Physical % estimate can be just as subjective (or gameable) as a time-based number.
reasoning: A learning-curve or front/back-loaded activity is the classic case where Duration % and Physical % diverge sharply: half the calendar time elapsed does not mean half the real output achieved. Units % ties most directly to labor-hour burn and cost performance. None of the three are interchangeable, and none are automatically trustworthy without a real measurement basis behind them.
commonMistakes: Assuming Physical % Complete is always more accurate simply because it's a separate manual field.
Believing the three percent types must always agree for a well-run project.
Not knowing that Duration % Complete is a calculated, not typed, field when that Percent Complete Type is active.
redFlags: Cannot name a real scenario where the three percentages would diverge.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: check the Percent Complete Type setting per activity before interpreting its %.
Check whether Physical % Complete entries are cross-referenced against a quantities/progress measurement system, not just estimated by eye.

followUpQuestions.prompt: On a lump-sum design-and-build tower crane erection activity with only two real milestones (delivered, commissioned), which percent-complete type would you recommend, and why?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests application of the concept to a non-linear, milestone-driven activity.

subcategory: Physical % vs Duration % vs Units % Complete
skill: Diagnosing over-reporting risk when Duration % Complete is used as a proxy for real physical progress
scenario: A subsea pipeline coating and wrapping activity is set to Duration percent-complete type. At this update it shows 90% Duration Complete (Actual Duration 27 of an At Completion Duration of 30 days). A site quality report from the same date estimates the physically wrapped and inspected length at only about 50% of the total run.
question: What is most likely happening here, and what would you do about it before this figure goes into the monthly progress report?
expectedAnswer: Duration % Complete is purely time-elapsed based; it says nothing about actual output. The crew has consumed 90% of the estimated calendar time but genuinely produced only about half the physical work — likely because productivity has been lower than planned (harder wrapping sections, rework, access constraints) while Remaining Duration was not re-forecast to reflect that reality. Before reporting, switch the narrative (and ideally the reported %) to the physically verified figure, and re-forecast Remaining Duration bottom-up from the actual production rate rather than letting it coast toward zero on a time-only basis.
strongAnswer: Adds that this is a genuine forecast risk, not just a reporting nuance: at the current output rate, the activity is very unlikely to finish within the remaining 3 days implied by the current Remaining Duration, so the forecast finish (and anything downstream/critical fed by it) is understated and needs correcting now, not discovered later.
expertAnswer: Notes the systemic fix: this activity should be switched to Physical % Complete (or resource/Units-based) tied to the quality-verified wrapped length, precisely because Duration-type activities with variable productivity are prone to this failure mode; also flags that if this pattern shows up across multiple activities, it indicates the project's percent-complete policy needs revisiting, not just this one activity's number.
explanation: This is the classic risk of using a purely time-based percent-complete type on effort/output-variable work: the number can look healthy right up until the forecast finish date arrives and the work simply isn't done, because nothing about Duration % Complete accounts for productivity actually achieved.
reasoning: Duration % Complete = Actual Duration / At Completion Duration, with no reference to units of output. If Remaining Duration is left unchanged (or reduced only slightly) each period regardless of true production rate, the percentage keeps climbing toward 100% on schedule while the real physical work lags — a silent divergence that typically surfaces as a sudden, large slip right before the planned finish.
commonMistakes: Reporting the 90% Duration figure as if it represents real progress.
Not cross-checking a Duration-type percentage against any independent physical measure before publishing it.
Assuming the gap will simply close itself as the remaining days are worked.
redFlags: Sees no problem with reporting 90% when physical evidence shows roughly half done.
Does not connect this to forecast finish date risk.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: check Percent Complete Type and consider switching this activity to Physical or Units.

Compare Remaining Duration's history period-over-period against the site's actual production rate (length wrapped per day) to test whether it has been genuinely re-forecast or just decremented mechanically.
Trace this activity's downstream successors to see if the forecast finish date optimism is propagating onto the critical path.

question: Which combination of fields correctly makes an activity 'Completed' in P6?

Zeroing Remaining Duration or pushing % Complete to 100% without an Actual Finish leaves the activity in an inconsistent, still-technically-'in progress' state that can confuse downstream reporting and earned value.
reasoning: P6's status logic reads the presence/absence of Actual Start and Actual Finish, not Remaining Duration or % Complete alone, to determine Not Started / In Progress / Completed.

skill: Using Suspend/Resume dates correctly for event-driven stoppages rather than folding them into Remaining Duration
scenario: You are updating the schedule for offshore monopile foundation installation. A storm closed the marine spread for 9 consecutive calendar days (no vessel access). The affected activity, 'Monopile Driving - WTG-14' (Original Duration 5 days), had already consumed 3 days of Actual Duration and was about 60% physically complete before the storm hit.
question: Explain how you would record this stoppage in P6, and why using the Suspend and Resume date fields is preferable to simply adding 9 days onto the activity's Remaining Duration.
expectedAnswer: Enter a Suspend date on the day work stopped and a Resume date on the day the marine spread remobilized; P6 will not schedule progress on the activity during that window, leaving a visible gap in the bar. This is preferable to just adding 9 days to Remaining Duration because it creates an explicit, auditable non-working period tied to a stated cause, rather than silently inflating the remaining-work estimate.
strongAnswer: Notes that inflating Remaining Duration instead would permanently mix an event-driven weather delay with the crew's actual productivity estimate, making it impossible later to separate 'time lost to weather' from 'time genuinely needed to finish the driving operation' — which matters if the productivity estimate needs revisiting again next period.
expertAnswer: Adds that this distinction matters commercially too: a storm closure is the kind of event that may later support an excusable-delay or weather-day claim under the contract, and a clean Suspend/Resume record with a dated cause is far stronger supporting evidence than a lump-sum remaining-duration adjustment with no documented reason.
explanation: Suspend/Resume exists specifically to record discrete, cause-attributable stoppages separately from the ordinary re-forecasting of remaining work, preserving both schedule integrity and an auditable record.
reasoning: The activity's underlying productivity/remaining-work estimate (how many more days of actual driving effort are needed) is a separate question from how many calendar days were lost to an external event. Suspend/Resume keeps those two numbers distinct; manually padding Remaining Duration conflates them and destroys the record of why the extra time was needed.
commonMistakes: Adding the 9 lost days directly onto Remaining Duration instead of using Suspend/Resume.
Using Suspend/Resume but not documenting the specific event/cause anywhere for later reference.
Forgetting to check whether the activity's calendar already treats storm-prone periods as non-working, which would double-count the delay.
redFlags: No distinction at all between an event-driven stoppage and routine remaining-duration re-forecasting.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: Suspend and Resume date fields on the in-progress activity.
Confirm the recalculated bar shows a genuine non-working gap between Suspend and Resume with no progress accruing in between.
Check that a delay/weather log entry or narrative reference is attached for later forensic or claims use.

skill: Diagnosing the likely real-world cause behind an out-of-sequence progress flag
scenario: After the weekly update on a data-center fit-out, P6 flags 'Cable Tray Installation - Room 3' as having out-of-sequence progress. Its Finish-to-Start predecessor, 'Raised Access Floor Installation - Room 3', is only 70% complete.
question: What is the most likely real-world explanation for this flag, and does it necessarily mean someone made a scheduling mistake?
expectedAnswer: Most likely the electrical subcontractor began installing cable tray in the portion of the room where flooring is already finished, while the flooring crew continues in the remaining area — genuinely concurrent execution that a strict Finish-to-Start tie didn't anticipate. It is not necessarily a scheduling mistake.
strongAnswer: Explains that whether it's a 'mistake' depends on intent: if this zone-by-zone overlap is a deliberate, repeatable execution strategy, the logic itself should be corrected (e.g., a Start-to-Start relationship with an appropriate lag, or splitting the floor activity by sub-area); if it was an uncoordinated shortcut with real risk to the unflored area's tray work, it's a genuine sequencing risk worth flagging to site management.
explanation: Out-of-sequence flags are a symptom, not a verdict — the same flag can indicate either a logic model that doesn't match legitimate real execution, or a genuine, un-planned deviation carrying risk. The planner's job is to find out which.
reasoning: A Finish-to-Start relationship assumes the predecessor must be fully finished before the successor starts anywhere. Partial, zone-based overlap is common in fit-out trades and is often a sound execution strategy that the original logic simply modeled too strictly.
commonMistakes: Assuming every out-of-sequence flag is a data-entry or planning error.
Assuming every out-of-sequence flag is fine and needs no follow-up because 'the crew knows what they're doing'.
redFlags: Treats the flag as purely cosmetic with no need to investigate the real cause.
p6Checks: Activities view, filter for out-of-sequence progress and inspect the specific predecessor relationship type and lag.
Talk to site supervision to confirm whether the overlap is a deliberate zone-based strategy.
Consider whether splitting the floor activity by sub-area would make the logic match reality going forward.

skill: Prioritizing and investigating a batch of out-of-sequence progress flags after a schedule update
scenario: Following this month's update on a metro tunnel TBM drive, the schedule now shows 14 activities flagged as having out-of-sequence progress, more than any prior month.
question: Before deciding whether to fix logic, leave it to the Retained Logic/Progress Override setting, or escalate it, what would you check first?
expectedAnswer: Confirm the project's current Out-of-Sequence Progress calculation setting (Retained Logic vs Progress Override), since it changes how each flagged activity's remaining work is being forecast right now. Then review each flagged relationship individually to classify it: modeling issue (wrong relationship type or missing lag), deliberate concurrent execution, or a genuine field-driven sequence break. Prioritize investigation by schedule impact — whether the flagged activities or their predecessors are on or near the critical path — rather than treating all 14 equally, and check whether the count has been trending up over recent periods (a systemic pattern, not just this month's noise).
strongAnswer: Adds that a sudden jump to 14 (versus a handful in prior months) is itself a signal worth investigating as a trend — it could indicate a broader execution strategy shift (e.g., an acceleration plan working multiple faces in parallel) that the logic network hasn't been updated to reflect.
expertAnswer: Notes that before recommending any blanket fix, they would confirm whether the project's OOS setting is contractually agreed or has been consistent throughout the project life, since changing it now to 'clean up' the flags would alter float and forecast dates without any real field change — a decision that needs client/commercial awareness, not just a scheduling convenience call.
explanation: A spike in out-of-sequence flags is a diagnostic signal, not something to blanket-fix with a global calculation setting. The competent response is triage: understand the setting currently in effect, classify each flagged case, prioritize by criticality, and look for a trend before acting.
reasoning: Out-of-sequence activities can be low-risk noise (non-critical zone overlaps) or genuine early warning of a network logic model that no longer matches how the project is actually being executed, which matters most where it touches the critical or near-critical path.
commonMistakes: Immediately switching the project-wide OOS setting to make the flags 'go away' without investigating causes.
Treating all 14 flags as equally important regardless of their proximity to the critical path.
Not checking whether this is a new spike or a long-running pattern.
redFlags: Wants to fix this purely by flipping a calculation setting with no investigation.

Activities view, filter 'Activities with out-of-sequence progress', sort by Total Float to prioritize.
Compare this month's OOS count against the trend from the last several updates.

skill: Correctly stating the mechanical consequences of the Retained Logic and Progress Override calculation settings
question: Which of the following statements about P6's Retained Logic and Progress Override out-of-sequence calculation settings are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: Retained Logic can cause the remaining (unexecuted) portion of an out-of-sequence activity's bar to be pushed and split, resuming only after its predecessor's logic constraint is satisfied.

options.label: B
options.text: Progress Override lets the remaining work of an out-of-sequence activity proceed forward from the Data Date without being interrupted by the still-unfinished predecessor relationship.

options.label: C
options.text: This setting is applied per individual activity, so different activities in the same project can use different rules with no project-wide effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither setting changes any calculated date or float value; they only change the color the out-of-sequence activity is drawn on the Gantt chart.

options.label: E
options.text: Switching the project-wide setting from one option to the other and recalculating can change forecast dates and float for out-of-sequence-affected activities even though no new field progress was entered.

explanation: Retained Logic and Progress Override are project-level Schedule Options that change how the scheduling engine treats the unexecuted portion of an out-of-sequence activity relative to its still-open predecessor relationship. Retained Logic keeps honoring that relationship for the remaining work (potentially splitting the bar); Progress Override lets the remaining work proceed unconstrained by it. Because this is a project-wide calculation setting, flipping it recalculates every affected activity's forecast — a real change in output with zero new field data.
reasoning: The two options answer the same question differently: 'for the part of this activity that has NOT yet happened, do we still enforce the logic tie to the unfinished predecessor, or not?' Retained Logic says yes (potentially conservative/pessimistic, can create odd gaps); Progress Override says no (potentially optimistic, can mask a genuine downstream logic risk).
commonMistakes: Believing the setting is chosen activity-by-activity rather than project-wide.
Believing the setting is purely cosmetic and doesn't affect calculated dates or float.
redFlags: Cannot explain the practical difference between the two settings at all.
p6Checks: Schedule Options dialog (accessed from the Schedule/F9 command): the Out of Sequence Progress control (Retain Logic / Progress Override / Actual Dates depending on version).

followUpQuestions.prompt: Which setting would you generally recommend as the project default, and why?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate has a defensible default position (commonly Retained Logic, as the more conservative/traceable default) while recognizing it's a judgment call, not a universal rule.

skill: Explaining how a pure calculation-setting change, with no new field data, can produce a large swing in forecast finish date and float
scenario: On an LNG terminal EPC schedule, the planning team switches the project's Out-of-Sequence Progress setting from Retained Logic to Progress Override mid-project, intending only to 'clean up' a batch of split activity bars. No field progress data is changed. The next schedule run shows the calculated project finish date pull in by 11 days, and several activities' Total Float increase by similar amounts.
question: Explain how a pure calculation-option change, with zero new field progress, produced an 11-day swing in the forecast finish date and float values. If this schedule is due for the monthly client submission, what would you do?
expectedAnswer: Retained Logic had been forcing the remaining, unexecuted portions of several out-of-sequence activities to wait until their still-open predecessors finished, which was pushing their remaining work (and everything downstream of it) later and consuming float on paths that pass through them. Progress Override releases that constraint, letting the same remaining work proceed immediately from the Data Date regardless of the unfinished predecessor — which is why dates pulled in and float increased, without a single day of real field progress changing.
strongAnswer: Explains this is not 'the schedule got better' — it's the schedule reporting a more optimistic view of the same underlying facts, because the still-unfinished predecessors have not actually gone away; the risk they represent (the successors' remaining work genuinely may still depend on them finishing) hasn't been resolved, only hidden from the current calculation.
expertAnswer: States they would not submit the schedule on the new setting without disclosure: at minimum, flag the setting change explicitly in the submission narrative with a before/after comparison, and ideally revert to Retained Logic (or investigate and fix the underlying logic properly, activity by activity) rather than let an 11-day improvement reach the client that isn't backed by real progress — since an undisclosed calculation-setting change that improves the reported finish date is exactly the kind of thing a forensic schedule reviewer would flag as manipulation, even if unintentional.
explanation: This is a genuine and important P6 trap: Retained Logic and Progress Override are project-wide calculation choices, not passive display options, and switching between them recalculates dates and float for every out-of-sequence-affected activity. A finish date or float improvement produced this way reflects a change in how the schedule is calculated, not a change in what has actually happened on site.
reasoning: Because Retained Logic enforces unfinished predecessor logic on remaining OOS work and Progress Override does not, the same underlying facts (which activities have started, how much is left) produce different forecast dates and float depending purely on which rule is applied. This is a calculation artifact, not new information.
commonMistakes: Treating the improved finish date as genuine progress.
Not recognizing the setting change is the entire cause of the 11-day swing.
Submitting the new schedule to the client without disclosing that the calculation basis changed.
redFlags: Sees nothing wrong with quietly submitting the more favorable result.
Cannot explain the mechanism at all and just calls it 'a P6 glitch'.
p6Checks: Schedule Options dialog: confirm and document the setting both before and after the change.
Run the schedule under both settings and compare the finish date/float delta directly to quantify the artifact.
Check whether the project's contract or governing procedure specifies (or requires consistency of) the OOS calculation setting.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can propose the real fix — reviewing and correcting logic activity by activity.

skill: Diagnosing a stale/unrevised Remaining Duration as the cause of an inflated At Completion Duration
scenario: An HVAC ductwork installation activity had an Original Duration of 15 days. At this update, Actual Duration shows 15 elapsed working days (the Data Date has reached the planned finish), but Remaining Duration still shows 6 days, unchanged from two update periods ago, and no Actual Finish has been entered — giving an At Completion Duration of 21 days, even though the site foreman reports the crew is nearly done.
question: What is the most likely cause of this inconsistency, and what should the planner have done differently at each intervening update?
expectedAnswer: Remaining Duration was left static across at least two update cycles instead of being actively re-forecast each period from field status, so it never converged toward zero even as Actual Duration kept climbing. The planner should re-estimate Remaining Duration bottom-up, from genuine current field status, at every single update, not just when a milestone or Actual Finish is being entered.
strongAnswer: Notes this pattern is especially likely when Percent Complete Type is set to Physical, since Physical % Complete does not automatically adjust Remaining Duration — the two fields are independent, and a planner focused only on entering the physical percentage can forget Remaining Duration needs separate attention.
explanation: A Remaining Duration value that doesn't move for multiple periods while Actual Duration keeps accumulating is a classic sign of a planner mechanically carrying forward last period's number rather than genuinely re-forecasting, and it silently inflates At Completion Duration and the forecast finish date.
reasoning: At Completion Duration = Actual Duration + Remaining Duration. If Remaining Duration isn't actively revised downward as real work is completed, At Completion Duration keeps growing even though the activity is, per the field, nearly finished — an internally inconsistent and misleading state.
commonMistakes: Carrying forward last period's Remaining Duration value without re-checking it against current field status.
Assuming Remaining Duration will auto-adjust when Physical % Complete is updated (it does not).
redFlags: Does not see anything wrong with a Remaining Duration value that hasn't moved in two periods.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: compare Remaining Duration's value against the prior two periods to check whether it has genuinely been revised.
Confirm the Percent Complete Type and whether Remaining Duration is meant to be manually maintained independently.

skill: Tracing the downstream consequences of forgetting to advance the Data Date before recalculating an update
scenario: A planner on an airport apron paving project entered this month's field progress, including several Actual Finish dates within the reporting month, but forgot to advance the project's Data Date from last month's value before running Schedule (F9).
question: What problems will this create in the resulting schedule, and how would you detect after the fact that this happened?
expectedAnswer: Some newly entered actual dates now sit later than the (stale) Data Date, which is an inconsistent state P6 will flag; forecast start dates for not-yet-started activities are still calculated from the old Data Date, understating how much of the period has actually elapsed; Total Float and critical path are calculated relative to the wrong 'as of today,' misrepresenting current schedule health; any progress curve or S-curve report generated from this run is mis-dated. Detect it by comparing the Data Date field against the intended period-end date, and by checking for any actual dates falling after the current Data Date.
strongAnswer: Adds that a quick sanity check is comparing the schedule's calculated forecast start dates for not-yet-started work against 'today' — if forecast starts look implausibly close to the old status date rather than reflecting the real elapsed time, that's a strong sign the Data Date wasn't moved.
explanation: The Data Date anchors the entire forward pass for remaining/forecast work. Leaving it stale while entering new actuals produces an internally inconsistent schedule where recorded facts and calculated forecasts are talking about two different 'as of' points.
reasoning: P6 treats the Data Date as the single dividing line between history and forecast. If it isn't advanced, remaining-work calculations effectively still think the update period hasn't happened yet, even though actual dates within it were entered.
commonMistakes: Not noticing the Data Date field wasn't changed before running the schedule.
Assuming entering actual dates alone is sufficient to 'move the schedule forward'.
redFlags: Does not understand why Data Date placement matters to the calculation, only that it's a reporting label.
p6Checks: Schedule (F9) dialog: verify the Data Date value before every recalculation.
Activities view: filter for actual dates later than the current Data Date.
Compare this period's forecast start dates for un-started activities against the expected elapsed time.

skill: Producing correct P6 status entries under a fast-track weekly cadence, including recognizing rework-driven progress and an out-of-sequence condition in the same cycle
scenario:
Weekly Data Date moves from 2026-03-06 to 2026-03-13 on Floor 22. You have the following field input:
- 'Chilled Water Piping - Floor 22' (Original Duration 5d, Finish-to-Start predecessor to Diffuser Installation): last week it was 20% physical complete (1 day Actual Duration, 4 days Remaining Duration). This week the riser team logged 3 more elapsed days but a design coordination clash forced rework of 2 days' worth of already-installed pipe; the QA/QC quantities survey now assesses true physical completion at only 35%.
- 'Diffuser Installation - Floor 22' (Original Duration 3d): was Not Started last week. This week, with site coordination approval, the diffuser crew started 1 day of work in a corridor where piping is already finished, achieving roughly 25% units complete, even though the piping activity overall is not yet finished.
- 'Fire Damper Testing - Floor 22' (Original Duration 2d): remains Not Started, no change this week.
requiredAnalysis: Determine the correct P6 status entries for each activity and identify both the rework-driven progress anomaly and the out-of-sequence condition.
question: State the correct P6 entries for each activity at the 2026-03-13 weekly update. Then explain (a) why the Chilled Water Piping activity's reported progress will look surprising compared to a naive 'more days elapsed, more percent complete' expectation, and why 35% is still the correct number to enter, and (b) which activity requires special handling for an out-of-sequence condition, and why.
expectedDecision: Chilled Water Piping: no Actual Finish; Remaining Duration and % Complete both re-forecast from the QA/QC survey to reflect true physical status (35%), even though 4 elapsed working days have now passed against a 5-day Original Duration — the rework means real progress is behind what elapsed time alone would suggest, and that lower number must be reported, not smoothed upward. Diffuser Installation: Actual Start entered as this week's start date, with a % Complete around 25% reflecting the corridor completed; this activity is the out-of-sequence case, since it has recorded actual progress while its Finish-to-Start predecessor (Chilled Water Piping) is not yet complete. Fire Damper Testing: no change, remains Not Started.
expectedAnswer: Correctly produces all three sets of entries, explains that rework legitimately reduces or caps true physical progress relative to elapsed time and that the lower, field-verified number must still be reported, and correctly identifies and names the Diffuser Installation activity's out-of-sequence condition.
strongAnswer: Adds that the Chilled Water Piping activity's Remaining Duration should be re-forecast bottom-up (likely more than the original 1 day left, given the rework) rather than assumed to be nearly finished just because 4 of 5 planned days have elapsed.
expertAnswer: Notes that the rework itself is a piece of information worth flagging in the update narrative (a design coordination clash causing rework is a potential cost/schedule issue worth raising early, separate from just adjusting the numbers), and that the out-of-sequence diffuser work should prompt a check on whether the corridor-by-corridor overlap should become a permanent logic change (e.g., splitting the piping activity by corridor) given it appears to be a deliberate coordination decision, not an accident.
explanation: This cycle combines two distinct real update challenges in one pass: recognizing that rework can legitimately make physical progress lag behind elapsed time (and that this must be reported honestly, not glossed over), and recognizing a genuine out-of-sequence condition created by a deliberate partial-area overlap.
reasoning: Physical/units-based percent complete reflects true output, which rework can reduce or hold back regardless of calendar days consumed. Out-of-sequence progress arises whenever a successor's actual progress precedes satisfaction of its predecessor relationship, exactly as with the diffuser crew working ahead of full piping completion.
commonMistakes: Reporting Chilled Water Piping near 100% because 4 of 5 planned days have elapsed, ignoring the rework.
Not recognizing the diffuser activity as out-of-sequence because 'the crew was only working in a finished corridor'.
Treating the rework as a private field issue not worth surfacing in the weekly report.
redFlags: Smooths over the rework to make the piping activity's percentage look better than the QA/QC survey supports.
Misses the out-of-sequence condition entirely.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: confirm Chilled Water Piping's % Complete matches the QA/QC survey, not a naive elapsed-time estimate.
Filter for 'Activities with out-of-sequence progress' after recalculating to confirm Diffuser Installation is flagged.

subcategory: Physical % vs Duration % vs Units % Complete
skill: Resolving a conflict between field-verified physical progress and a schedule-calculated Duration % Complete figure
scenario: On a solar farm racking installation package, the field QA/QC quantities survey shows 40% of the racking physically erected and bolted. The P6 activity is set to Duration percent-complete type and is currently calculating 55% Duration Complete, based on elapsed time and a Remaining Duration figure entered two periods ago.
question: Which figure do you report as the activity's progress this period, and what do you do about the schedule itself?
expectedAnswer: Report the field-verified physical figure (40%), since it reflects real output rather than elapsed time. Correct the schedule by re-forecasting Remaining Duration so that Duration % Complete becomes consistent with the physical evidence (i.e., increase Remaining Duration to reflect the true, slower pace) rather than letting a stale Duration-based number stay artificially ahead of reality.
strongAnswer: Recommends considering switching this activity's Percent Complete Type to Physical or Units going forward if this kind of divergence is likely to recur, so the schedule stays self-consistent with field evidence without requiring a manual correction every period.
expertAnswer: Adds that the 15-point gap should also prompt a check of whether the forecast finish date and any downstream critical activities fed by this one are now understated, since the schedule has effectively been reporting more progress than actually exists for at least one period, and flags this as a pattern to watch for in other Duration-type activities on the same package.
explanation: Where a field-verified, quantities-based measure conflicts with a purely time-based calculated percentage, the field-verified figure should govern reporting, and the schedule itself should be corrected to match it rather than left inconsistent.
reasoning: Duration % Complete only reflects elapsed calendar time against a (possibly stale) Remaining Duration estimate; it has no connection to actual output. A quantities-based physical survey is a direct measurement of real progress and should take priority whenever the two disagree.
commonMistakes: Reporting the higher, more favorable Duration % Complete figure because it's already in the system.
Correcting the reported percentage but leaving Remaining Duration unchanged, so the schedule reverts to the same wrong number next period.
redFlags: Chooses to report whichever number looks better rather than the one supported by evidence.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: check Percent Complete Type and consider changing it to Physical or Units.
Update Remaining Duration to be consistent with the physical survey, then verify the recalculated Duration % Complete matches expectations.

skill: Calculating Units % Complete from actual and budgeted labor-hours
scenario: A rebar-fixing package has a budgeted (at-completion) resource loading of 4,200 labor-hours. As of this update, verified timesheets show 1,890 labor-hours have actually been expended on the activity.
question: Calculate the Units % Complete for this activity.
explanation: Units % Complete = Actual Units / At Completion Units x 100 = 1,890 / 4,200 x 100 = 45%.
reasoning: Units % Complete ties directly to resource/labor-hour consumption rather than elapsed calendar time or an independently entered physical estimate, which makes it useful for cost-linked or productivity-driven activities where labor-hour burn is a meaningful proxy for progress.
commonMistakes: Dividing the budgeted hours by the actual hours instead of the reverse.
Confusing Units % Complete with Duration % Complete when the activity's Percent Complete Type is actually set to Units.

skill: Distinguishing the fixed planned Original Duration field from the dynamic At Completion Duration
question: Once an activity has been progressed over several update periods, which statement about its Original Duration field is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Original Duration automatically updates each period to match the sum of Actual Duration and Remaining Duration

options.label: B
options.text: Original Duration stays fixed at the planned value first entered when the activity was built into the schedule, and only changes if a planner explicitly edits it (e.g., an approved scope or logic change)

options.label: C
options.text: Original Duration is cleared automatically once an Actual Finish date is entered

options.label: D
options.text: Original Duration always equals Remaining Duration once the activity starts

explanation: Original Duration is the planned reference value and is not recalculated by status entries; only At Completion Duration (Actual Duration + Remaining Duration) moves as the activity is progressed and re-forecast. Keeping Original Duration fixed is what makes it possible to later compare the current forecast against what was originally planned.
reasoning: Separating the fixed plan (Original Duration) from the live forecast (At Completion Duration) is what allows meaningful performance comparison — if Original Duration silently moved with every status update, there would be no stable baseline reference left within the activity itself.
commonMistakes: Believing Original Duration tracks along with Remaining Duration as work progresses.
Confusing Original Duration with At Completion Duration.
redFlags: Cannot explain why keeping Original Duration fixed matters.

skill: Recognizing an internally inconsistent Actual Finish / Remaining Duration / % Complete combination
scenario: An activity 'Underground Duct Bank Backfill' shows an Actual Finish date of 2026-04-10 entered, but its Remaining Duration field still shows 2 days rather than zero, and % Complete shows 92%.
question: Is this a valid, internally consistent state? What is most likely happening, and how should it be corrected?
expectedAnswer: This is not consistent: once an Actual Finish is entered, the activity should be Completed, with % Complete at 100 and Remaining Duration at zero. A non-zero Remaining Duration and 92% alongside an Actual Finish most likely means the Actual Finish was entered prematurely (e.g., to close the activity out for reporting optics) while roughly 2 days of work genuinely remain, or that the planner forgot to zero Remaining Duration and finalize % Complete after typing the Actual Finish date.
strongAnswer: Recommends going back to the source: confirm with site whether the work is truly 100% finished (if so, correct Remaining Duration to 0 and % Complete to 100) or genuinely not finished (in which case the Actual Finish date should be removed and the activity kept In Progress with an honest Remaining Duration and % Complete).
explanation: P6 does not enforce that these three fields stay mutually consistent in real time as a user types them, so a record like this can exist in the file, but it represents either a premature Actual Finish entry or an incomplete correction, not a genuine finished state.
reasoning: By definition, Completed status (Actual Finish present) implies no work remains — Remaining Duration should be zero and % Complete should be 100. Any other combination signals the entry doesn't reflect the true state of the work and needs to be reconciled against what site actually reports.
commonMistakes: Accepting the Actual Finish date at face value without checking whether Remaining Duration and % Complete were actually finalized.
Assuming this combination is a P6 bug rather than a data-entry inconsistency to investigate.
redFlags: Sees nothing wrong with a Completed activity that still shows remaining work.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: cross-check Actual Finish against Remaining Duration and % Complete together, not one field in isolation.
Confirm with the field team whether the activity is genuinely finished before correcting the record either way.

skill: Diagnosing an unexplained critical path shift after a routine update by tracing float trends rather than assuming an error
scenario: Before this month's update on a petrochemical plant expansion, the critical path ran through the structural steel erection package. After this month's update - with no major logic changes recorded and unremarkable field progress reported - the critical path shifted entirely to the fire protection commissioning package, whose Total Float dropped from +18 days to 0.
question: What is the most likely explanation for the critical path suddenly reappearing on a completely different package, and what would you check to confirm it?
expectedAnswer: Most likely, the steel erection package genuinely progressed to (or near) completion this period, freeing up that path from being critical, while the fire protection package's float had actually been eroding gradually over several prior periods without drawing attention (because its finish-date variance was small and no one was tracking float trend, only finish dates) - this update simply crossed the point where its float reached zero and it became visibly critical. It is not necessarily an error; it can be the ordinary, if under-monitored, result of float erosion finally becoming visible.

The competent response is to verify with float-trend data, not assume a scheduling error.
reasoning: Total Float reaching zero is often the visible end-point of a gradual erosion process rather than a single-period event; tracking only finish-date variance can miss this because a path can be losing float every period while its calculated finish date barely moves, right up until float hits zero and it becomes critical, at which point the finish date starts moving too.

Only comparing this period's snapshot without pulling prior periods' float history.

skill: Correctly stating P6's Duration % Complete formula
question: Which formula correctly expresses how P6 calculates Duration % Complete for an activity using that percent-complete type?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual Duration / Original Duration x 100

options.label: B
options.text: Actual Duration / (Actual Duration + Remaining Duration) x 100

options.label: C
options.text: Remaining Duration / Original Duration x 100

options.label: D
options.text: (Original Duration - Remaining Duration) / Original Duration x 100

explanation: Duration % Complete = Actual Duration / At Completion Duration x 100, where At Completion Duration = Actual Duration + Remaining Duration. It is not based on Original Duration, which is why the two can diverge once Remaining Duration is re-forecast away from the original plan.
reasoning: Using Original Duration as the denominator (options A, C, D) is a common trap because it feels intuitive, but it ignores that Remaining Duration is frequently re-forecast to a different value than 'Original Duration minus elapsed,' which is exactly the point of active status updates.
commonMistakes: Using Original Duration instead of At Completion Duration as the denominator.
Assuming the formula is fixed to Original Duration and therefore that Duration % Complete can never exceed what elapsed time against the original plan would suggest.
redFlags: Cannot state the correct denominator at all.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If Remaining Duration is re-forecast lower than 'Original Duration minus Actual Duration', what happens to At Completion Duration and Duration % Complete?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Remedial prompt toward the correct formula.

skill: Handling the gap between physical completion and pending administrative sign-off without corrupting the schedule status
scenario: An earthworks activity 'Cut to Fill - Pad C' reached 100% physical completion per the site survey two weeks ago, but the planner only updated % Complete to 100 and left Actual Finish blank, because the formal compaction test certificate has not yet been issued.
question: What problems can leaving Actual Finish blank in this situation create downstream, and what is the correct way to handle physical completion that is pending formal sign-off?
expectedAnswer: Leaving Actual Finish blank keeps the activity technically In Progress indefinitely, which misrepresents true close-out status in progress reports, S-curves, and any earned-value cutoff logic that filters on Completed status, and leaves no clean record of when physical work actually stopped if the certificate is delayed or the test needs to be repeated. The correct handling is to enter the Actual Finish as of the date physical work was verified complete, and track the outstanding certificate separately (e.g., as a distinct action item or milestone) rather than conflating physical completion with administrative sign-off by leaving the schedule activity artificially open.
strongAnswer: Notes this is a common and legitimate real-world situation (test/certification lag behind physical work) and that the fix is a process discipline point, not a one-off correction: physical completion and paperwork completion are two different facts and should never be forced into a single date field just because one is more convenient to track than the other.
explanation: An activity's Actual Finish should reflect when the physical scope was genuinely finished, not when every piece of paperwork clears — otherwise the schedule silently drifts from reality every time certification lags behind fieldwork, which is common on quality-gated activities.
reasoning: P6 uses the presence of Actual Finish to determine Completed status, which in turn affects how successors, reports, and earned-value snapshots treat the activity. An activity stuck at 100% % Complete with no Actual Finish is an ambiguous, non-standard state that different reports may handle inconsistently.
commonMistakes: Leaving Actual Finish blank until every piece of paperwork is in hand, even when physical work is verifiably done.
Not creating any separate record/action item to track the still-outstanding certificate once Actual Finish is entered.
redFlags: Sees no issue with an activity sitting at 100% with no Actual Finish for weeks.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: check for activities at or near 100% % Complete with no Actual Finish date, as a routine data-quality scan.
Cross-check such activities against any outstanding quality/certification log to confirm the physical-vs-paperwork distinction is understood, not just missed.

skill: Recognizing that Remaining Duration should be a bottom-up field forecast, not a mechanical function of elapsed time
question: True or False: Remaining Duration should generally be re-forecast each period based on the actual scope of work still to do and current productivity, rather than mechanically calculated as Original Duration minus elapsed time.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: Original Duration minus elapsed time assumes the originally planned productivity rate holds exactly, which is rarely true in practice once rework, productivity variance, access constraints, or scope clarifications are factored in. Good practice treats Remaining Duration as a genuine forecast, re-estimated from current field status every period.
reasoning: Mechanically deriving Remaining Duration this way silently bakes in the assumption that nothing about the pace of work has changed since the plan was made — an assumption that is routinely wrong on real projects, which is exactly why disciplined bottom-up re-forecasting matters.
commonMistakes: Believing Remaining Duration should always just be 'what's left of the original plan' rather than a live forecast.

Confirm the project's current Retained Logic/Progress Override setting and how it is treating each one's forecast. Prioritize by proximity to the critical path. Fix logic where it's a genuine, repeatable modeling issue; document and flag the rest, especially any that represent real schedule risk. explanation: Multiple out-of-sequence flags in one cycle need a structured triage, not a single blanket action — classify, prioritize by criticality, fix what should be fixed, and document what can't or shouldn't be fixed this cycle, before the report is finalized.

skill: Identifying the range of genuine real-world causes of out-of-sequence progress
question: Which of the following are realistic causes of out-of-sequence progress appearing in a P6 schedule? Select all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: A relationship was modeled as Finish-to-Start when the real execution intent is a partial, zone-based Start-to-Start overlap between the two activities

options.label: B
options.text: A relationship is missing a lag, or has too short a lag, for work that trades genuinely need between the predecessor and successor

options.label: C
options.text: A deliberate, schedule-recovery decision to push a successor to start before its predecessor fully finishes, in order to protect an overall milestone

options.label: D
options.text: The activity's calendar was changed from a 5-day to a 6-day work week

options.label: E
options.text: A data-entry error where an Actual Start date was entered that does not match what actually happened in the field

explanation: Out-of-sequence progress arises whenever recorded actual progress on a successor doesn't respect its predecessor's logic tie as modeled. That can come from a logic model that doesn't match real execution intent, an under-specified relationship (missing lag), a deliberate commercial/recovery decision, or simple data-entry error. A calendar change (5-day to 6-day week) affects duration and dates but does not by itself cause an out-of-sequence condition.
reasoning: The common thread across the valid causes is a mismatch between what the network logic says must happen first and what actually happened first in the field or in the data entry — a calendar change alone doesn't create that mismatch.
commonMistakes: Assuming a calendar change is a typical cause of out-of-sequence progress.
Assuming out-of-sequence progress only ever comes from data-entry error, missing that deliberate execution strategy is a very common legitimate cause.
redFlags: Cannot name more than one plausible cause.

skill: Recognizing that Suspend/Resume only applies to already-started activities, and choosing the correct treatment when a delay hits a not-yet-started activity
scenario: A permit hold halted work related to an excavation package on an urban utility relocation project for 5 days. A junior planner asks whether they should reduce the excavation activity's Remaining Duration by 5 days to 'catch up' the schedule, or use the Suspend and Resume date fields instead.
question: What would you check first before answering the junior planner, and what is the correct guidance?
expectedAnswer: First check whether the excavation activity had already started (an Actual Start already recorded) before the permit hold occurred. Suspend/Resume only applies to an already in-progress activity; if the activity had not yet started, those fields don't apply at all, and the correct treatment is simply not to record an Actual Start until work genuinely begins, with the delay reflected as a later start rather than through Suspend/Resume. If the activity WAS already in progress when the hold occurred, then yes, Suspend/Resume (not a manual Remaining Duration cut) is the correct tool.
strongAnswer: Notes that in neither case should Remaining Duration simply be reduced to 'catch up' the schedule — that would misrepresent either a stoppage that should be explicitly recorded (if in progress) or a delayed start that should just show up as a later Actual Start (if not yet started).
explanation: Suspend/Resume is specifically for pausing an in-progress activity; it has no meaning for an activity that hasn't started. The first branch point in advising the junior planner is exactly this: was the activity in progress or not when the hold hit.
reasoning: Getting this wrong in either direction corrupts the record: applying Suspend/Resume to a not-yet-started activity is meaningless, and cutting Remaining Duration for either case misrepresents the delay as increased productivity rather than a real stoppage or late start.
commonMistakes: Assuming Suspend/Resume is the universal answer for any delay regardless of whether the activity had started.
Defaulting to 'just reduce Remaining Duration' as the simplest fix without checking activity status first.
redFlags: Gives a single blanket answer without asking whether the activity had started.
p6Checks: Activities view, Status tab: check for an existing Actual Start date on the excavation activity before deciding.
If in progress, use the Suspend and Resume fields; if not started, simply delay the Actual Start entry to when work genuinely begins.

skill: Calculating Total Float for a near-complete activity feeding a constrained milestone, from the Data Date forward
scenario: Activity 'Final MEP Testing - Substation 4' has 2 days of Remaining Duration as of the current Data Date, 2026-08-10 (a Monday). It uses a standard Monday-to-Friday working calendar with no holidays in this window. It is tied by a Finish-to-Start relationship to the milestone 'Substation 4 Energization Ready', which carries a Finish-on-or-before constraint of 2026-08-19.
question: Calculate the Total Float, in working days, of the Final MEP Testing activity. Show your calculation.
explanation: Early Finish: starting from the Data Date (2026-08-10, Monday), 2 remaining working days land on Tuesday 2026-08-11 and Wednesday 2026-08-12, so Early Finish = 2026-08-12. Late Finish is governed by the milestone's Finish-on-or-before constraint of 2026-08-19 (the following Wednesday). Counting working days from the Early Finish to the Late Finish (2026-08-13 Thu, 08-14 Fri, 08-17 Mon, 08-18 Tue, 08-19 Wed) gives 5 working days of Total Float.
reasoning: Total Float = Late Finish minus Early Finish, measured in the activity's calendar working days. The Data Date anchors the forward pass (Early Finish), and the imposed Finish-on-or-before constraint on the successor milestone anchors the backward pass (Late Finish) for this path.
commonMistakes: Counting calendar days instead of working days, which would overstate the float by including the intervening weekend.
Forgetting the milestone's constraint governs Late Finish and instead assuming Late Finish equals Early Finish (zero float) by default.
Miscounting the Early Finish by treating the Data Date itself as the first day of remaining work rather than the starting point from which remaining days are counted forward.
redFlags: Cannot explain why the Data Date, not some other date, is the starting point for the forward pass here.
p6Checks: Activities view: confirm the activity's assigned calendar (working days) before counting.
Check the milestone's constraint type and date directly in the Constraints field, not just its calculated Early Finish.
Verify Total Float shown in P6 matches this manual calculation as a sanity check on the calendar assignment.

skill: Responding to management pressure to falsely overstate progress in a P6 update

Site inspection actually confirms only about 90% of the scope is done - final MEP rough-in penetrations remain open in two rooms. The PM says: 'It'll be done by the time anyone checks, just show it green for the review.'
question: How do you respond to the project manager, and what do you actually enter in P6?

strongAnswer: Frames a constructive alternative rather than just refusing: present the true 90% figure with a clear, specific narrative on the two remaining rooms and their expected close-out date, which is still a strong, credible story for the review - arguably more credible than an unqualified 'complete' that could be publicly contradicted by a walkthrough.
expertAnswer: If the PM insists, escalates appropriately: documents the instruction and the actual field data, raises it with the PM's own management chain or the project controls lead rather than complying, and is explicit that this is not a judgment call on methodology (like which percent-complete type to use) but a request to report something false - a different category of issue.
